Have you ever made a cup of tea or coffee?

The process is always the same boil water, add the main ingredient, pour into a cup, add extras. The sequence never changes. But the details do. Tea uses tea leaves. Coffee uses coffee grounds. Tea gets lemon. Coffee gets milk.
This is exactly what the Template Method Pattern does.
It defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class the fixed sequence of steps. Subclasses fill in the details of specific steps without touching the overall structure.
Without Template Method:
boilWater() and pourInCup() are duplicated everywhere. Add a third drink and you copy the same structure again.
With Template Method:
The sequence lives in one place. Subclasses only override what is different.
It is useful when:
["Multiple classes share the same sequence of steps.","Only certain steps differ between implementations.","You want to avoid duplicating the overall algorithm in every subclass."]
items: Multiple classes share the same sequence of steps.
Only certain steps differ between implementations.
You want to avoid duplicating the overall algorithm in every subclass.

blocks.content: Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Processing Online Orders
Let's say you are building an e-commerce platform that processes orders differently based on the delivery type Standard, Express, and International.
Each order follows the same high-level workflow:

["Validate Order Check item availability and customer details","Calculate Cost Compute total price including delivery charges","Process Payment Charge the customer","Package Items Pack the order for shipment","Ship Order Dispatch using the appropriate carrier","Send Confirmation Notify the customer"]
items: Validate Order Check item availability and customer details
Calculate Cost Compute total price including delivery charges

blocks.content: The workflow is identical across all delivery types. Only the cost calculation and shipping step differ. But if you implement each processor independently, you end up duplicating all the shared logic every time.
Naive Approach

codes.python:
class StandardOrderProcessor:
    def process(self, order_id):
        print(f"Standard: Validating order {order_id}")
        # ... validation logic ...

        print("Standard: Calculating cost - base rate")
        # ... standard cost calculation ...

        print("Standard: Processing payment")
        # ... payment logic ...

        print("Standard: Packaging items")
        # ... packaging logic ...

        print("Standard: Shipping via postal service - 5 to 7 days")
        # ... standard shipping logic ...

        print("Standard: Sending confirmation email")
        # ... email logic ...


class ExpressOrderProcessor:
    def process(self, order_id):
        print(f"Express: Validating order {order_id}")
        # ... same validation logic copied ...

        print("Express: Calculating cost - base rate + express surcharge")
        # ... express cost calculation ...

        print("Express: Processing payment")
        # ... same payment logic copied ...

        print("Express: Packaging items")
        # ... same packaging logic copied ...

        print("Express: Shipping via express courier - same day")
        # ... express shipping logic ...

        print("Express: Sending confirmation email")
        # ... same email logic copied ...


class InternationalOrderProcessor:
    def process(self, order_id):
        print(f"International: Validating order {order_id}")
        # ... same validation logic copied again ...

        print("International: Calculating cost - base rate + customs + tax")
        # ... international cost calculation ...

        print("International: Processing payment")
        # ... same payment logic copied again ...

        print("International: Packaging items")
        # ... same packaging logic copied again ...

        print("International: Shipping via international freight")
        # ... international shipping logic ...

        print("International: Sending confirmation email")
        # ... same email logic copied again ...


if __name__ == "__main__":
    StandardOrderProcessor().process("ORD-001")
    ExpressOrderProcessor().process("ORD-002")
    InternationalOrderProcessor().process("ORD-003")

blocks.content: What's Wrong With This Design?

1. Code Duplication Validation, payment, packaging, and confirmation are copied verbatim into every processor. Add a fourth delivery type and you copy the same boilerplate again. Every duplicated line is a future bug waiting to happen.

2. Maintenance Overhead Need to add fraud detection before payment? Or change how confirmation emails are sent? You must make the same change in every processor class. Miss one and that delivery type silently behaves differently.

3. Inconsistent Behavior Nothing stops a developer from accidentally skipping a step, reordering them, or adding a step in one processor but not another. The system drifts toward inconsistency over time.

4. Poor Extensibility Adding a new delivery type means copying an entire class and tweaking a few lines. It is completely unclear which parts are shared logic and which parts are specific to each delivery type.
What We Really Need

["Define the common order processing workflow once in a single base class.","Allow subclasses to override only the format-specific steps cost calculation and shipping.","Enforce a consistent step ordering so no processor can accidentally skip or reorder steps.","Make adding a new delivery type as simple as creating one subclass with two method overrides."]
items: Define the common order processing workflow once in a single base class.
Allow subclasses to override only the format-specific steps cost calculation and shipping.
Enforce a consistent step ordering so no processor can accidentally skip or reorder steps.
Make adding a new delivery type as simple as creating one subclass with two method overrides.

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Template Method Pattern provides.
2. What is the Template Method Pattern?
blocks.text: 2. What is the Template Method Pattern?

blocks.content: The Template Method Pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and defers specific steps to subclasses. It keeps the overall structure of the process consistent while giving subclasses the flexibility to customize only the parts that differ.
Two characteristics define it:

1. Algorithm skeleton in the base class The base class contains a method the template method that defines the fixed sequence of steps. This method is marked final so subclasses cannot alter the order or skip steps.

2. Subclasses override specific steps The base class declares abstract methods for the steps that vary. Subclasses implement only those methods. They never control when those methods are called the template method handles that.

Real-World Analogy

Think of a car assembly line.

Every car sedan, SUV, or truck goes through the same assembly sequence: build the chassis, install the engine, fit the body, paint, install interiors, run quality checks.

The sequence never changes. But installing a truck engine is completely different from installing a sedan engine. Fitting an SUV body is different from fitting a sedan body. Each model fills in its own details but the assembly line always runs in the same order.

The Template Method Pattern works exactly the same way the base class owns the sequence, subclasses own the details.

blocks.content: The Key Participants

Abstract Class OrderProcessor Contains the template method processOrder() marked final the fixed sequence no subclass can reorder or skip. Declares abstract methods for steps that vary across delivery types calculateCost() and shipOrder(). Provides concrete implementations for shared steps validateOrder(), processPayment(), packageItems(), sendConfirmation(). Also provides hook methods like addInsurance() that subclasses can optionally override.

Concrete Classes StandardOrderProcessor, ExpressOrderProcessor, InternationalOrderProcessor Each extends OrderProcessorand provides its own implementation of only the abstract steps. Optionally overrides hook methods for extra behavior. Never touches the sequence that belongs to the base class.

Template Method processOrder() The final method in OrderProcessor that orchestrates the entire sequence. Mixes concrete steps owned by the base class with abstract steps filled in by subclasses and hook steps optionally customized.

Hooks addInsurance() A concrete method in the base class with an empty default implementation. Standard orders skip it. Express and International orders override it to add insurance. Provides an extension point without forcing every subclass to implement it.

Key Design Decision

We use an abstract class rather than an interface because the base class needs to provide a concrete template method with real logic the step ordering. An interface cannot contain a method that calls other methods in a fixed sequence while enforcing that sequence.

This is one of the few patterns where inheritance is the right tool not composition.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 3. How It Works
The Template Method workflow follows a clear delegation sequence:
Sequence Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245812664-69787162.png
Step 1 The client creates an instance of a concrete class StandardOrderProcessor, ExpressOrderProcessor, or InternationalOrderProcessor.
Step 2 The client calls the template method processOrder() on the concrete instance.
Step 3 The template method, defined in the abstract base class OrderProcessor, begins executing. It calls all steps in the fixed order defined by the skeleton.
Step 4 For shared steps validateOrder(), processPayment(), packageItems(), sendConfirmation() the base class implementation runs directly.
Step 5 For abstract steps calculateCost() and shipOrder() the call is dispatched to the concrete subclass's own implementation.

Step 6 For hook steps addInsurance()  the base class empty default runs unless the subclass has overridden it. ExpressOrderProcessor and InternationalOrderProcessor override it. StandardOrderProcessor does not.
Step 7 The template method completes. The client gets a consistent result regardless of which processor was used.
4. Implementing Template Method

Let's refactor the order processing system using the Template Method Pattern. The goal is to extract the common workflow into a single base class and let each delivery type override only the steps that differ.
Step 1: Create the Abstract Base Class

blocks.content: Step 2: Implement Concrete Processors
StandardOrderProcessor
Implements the two abstract steps. Does not override the hook standard orders have no insurance.
ExpressOrderProcessor
Implements abstract steps with express-specific logic. Overrides the hook to add insurance.
InternationalOrderProcessor
Implements abstract steps with international-specific logic. Also overrides the hook for customs insurance.
Notice the difference between ExpressOrderProcessor an StandardOrderProcessor. Both implement the two required abstract methods.

But only ExpressOrderProcessor andInternationalOrderProcessor override the addInsurance() hook  because standard orders do not need it. This is the power of hooks: subclasses opt into extra behavior without forcing every subclass to deal with it.

blocks.content: By applying the Template Method Pattern we have eliminated code duplication by moving the shared workflow into a single base class, enforced consistency by locking the step order in thefinaltemplate method,
made the system extensible adding aSameDayOrderProcessormeans one new subclass with two method overrides, and provided clear extension points through abstract methods (required) and hooks (optional).
5. Evolving the System: Adding a New Delivery Type
blocks.text: 5. Evolving the System: Adding a New Delivery Type

blocks.content: The real test of any pattern is what happens when requirements change. The business now wants a Same Day Deliveryoption. With the Template Method Pattern in place, this means creating one new subclass.
No changes to OrderProcessor, no changes toStandardOrderProcessor, ExpressOrderProcessor, or InternationalOrderProcessor.
That is the entire change. One new class, three method overrides, zero modifications to existing code.
The OrderProcessorbase class is untouched. All existing processors are untouched. This is the Open/Closed Principle at work open for extension, closed for modification.
